text:
You are one of 4 members of a group that stays together for 10 rounds.

Every round, all members act at the same time: each receives 20 tokens and splits them between their own account and the group account, using the split tool once.
- Each token in your own account pays you 1 point and lowers the points of every other member by 0.3. In the same way, every token another member keeps in their own account lowers your points by 0.3.
- Each token in the group account pays you 0.3 points and does not change any other member's points.
- Every round, every member also receives 18 points, whatever anyone does.

After each round you learn how many tokens the group account received in total and how many points you got. You never learn what any other member did.

calls.text: Round 1 of 10.

reply.thinking:
I'm working through the payoff structure of this public goods game: each member gets a flat 18 points, plus their kept tokens worth 1 each, minus 0.3 for every token every other member keeps.

The key insight is that moving one token from "kept" to "group account" changes my own payoff by -1 + 0.3 = -0.7, since I only get the 0.3 multiplier back on the group total but lose the full 1 point from keeping it. This means keeping tokens is individually optimal for my own payoff, even though contributing to the group benefits everyone collectively.

If everyone defects fully, each ends up with around 20 points, but if everyone cooperates fully, each could net around 42 — a clear social dilemma where individual incentives conflict with collective welfare. Since this is a 10-round repeated game with unknown counterparts, I'm weighing whether to signal cooperation early via trigger strategies, despite the personal cost of contributing tokens when others might keep everything.

For round one, I think the safer play is a moderate contribution — maybe 10 to the group — as a way to probe others' behavior without overcommitting, then adjust based on how the group responds.
